description: We are a young team from Costa Rica with one rule: ship working products, not slides. We built Afterglow to let anyone watch NASA's SPHEREx infrared sky change and trust what they see. We are ambitious and honest about it. Our first goal is to be Global Nominees, and then to go for Global Winner. Above all, we want to prove that Costa Rica has world class talent that can build real science tools at the level of anyone, anywhere.
summary:
Afterglow independently recovers real changes in NASA's SPHEREx infrared sky, and every result can be
  checked in one click. Our blind pipeline compared 345,952 measurements of 2,310 stars between April
  2025 and September 2026. After channel by channel calibration, neighbor rejection and a 5 sigma
  threshold, exactly one change survived: ZTF J175232.01+653228.6, an eclipsing binary already
  catalogued, recovered without telling the method where to look. Motion is just as verifiable:
  Afterglow measured Barnard's Star moving 10.24 arcsec between survey passes, and ESA's Gaia predicts
  10.27 arcsec. For Planet X, we hid fake planets in real SPHEREx images and measured how faint we can
  still recover them blind. One pass reaches AB 17.8, while Planet Nine is predicted at V 22 to 25,
  about 50 times fainter, so finding it needs roughly 2,000 stacked passes or a deeper telescope such as
  Rubin. The same method powers a public web tool. Type any coordinates or star name and Afterglow
  plays every SPHEREx image of that spot as a time lapse, subtracts passes to reveal what moved, steps
  through 102 infrared colors, marks known asteroids from NASA JPL and measures the spectrum on the fly.
  Anyone, with no account, can mark something across frames, and Afterglow turns those marks into a 
  measured motion. Afterglow lets anyone watch the infrared sky change, and trust what they see.
details:
What does it do?

SPHEREx maps the whole sky in 102 infrared channels every six months, but the raw data are thousands of files that need specialist software. Afterglow turns them into a public web tool: any spot of the infrared sky, over time, in a browser.


The tool

  • Any spot in the sky: type coordinates or a star name and Afterglow plays every SPHEREx image of that spot (Data Release 1 and Quick Release 3) as a time lapse, aligned north up.
  • Stack and difference: each pass is stacked per detector, and subtracting passes shows change. A moving star appears as a white and black pair.














  • What moved, checked against Gaia: every measured motion is shown next to the ESA Gaia DR3 prediction. Barnard's Star: 10.24 arcsec measured, 10.27 predicted.
  • Sources seen in only one pass: the signature of something that moved far or appeared. Each must show in two detectors and is checked against Gaia and known asteroids from NASA JPL. No false alarms in 47 real fields.
  • Spectrum on the fly: forced photometry on SPHEREx's 102 channel grid.
  • Play the 102 colors: the all sky cube played channel by channel.
  • Citizen reports: anyone can mark an object across frames, without an account, and get a fitted motion.
  • Planet Nine test: one button asks whether SPHEREx could see Planet Nine at that spot. Afterglow hides fake planets in the real images, shifted by Earth's real parallax between passes, and searches for them blind.

The pipeline

  • 2,310 stars near the north ecliptic pole, 345,952 measurements.
  • Both epochs calibrated channel by channel.
  • Stars with close or brighter neighbors removed.
  • Flagged: changes of at least 5 sigma in 3 or more channels.

What we found

One real change

  • Exactly one of 2,310 stars changed: ZTF J175232.01+653228.6, an eclipsing binary already catalogued.
  • The method did not know it was there.
  • Of the five challenge test objects, Afterglow marks as moving exactly the two Gaia says should move.





Could SPHEREx see Planet Nine?

  • We hid 5,040 fake planets in 9 real fields.
  • In quiet fields one pass recovers half of them down to AB 17.4 to 17.8.
  • Planet Nine is predicted at V 22 to 25, about 50 times fainter.
  • We report that limit, not a detection: it is the measured starting point for a deeper search.



Benefits

  • Raw SPHEREx files become images and measurements anyone can open in seconds.
  • Every claim links to its images, spectrum, IRSA viewer and Gaia comparison.
  • New releases are configuration, not code.

Intended impact

  • Education: real NASA infrared data for any target a student picks.
  • Citizen science: the blink view volunteers use to find brown dwarfs, now on SPHEREx.
  • Science: an open baseline for SPHEREx time domain work and a measured depth for a Planet Nine search.

Tools

  • Python: FastAPI, astropy, astroquery, photutils, numpy, scipy.
  • Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with Aladin Lite from CDS.
  • 73 automated tests, one Docker container.

Creativity and what we considered

  • We reproject every frame north up; without it, SPHEREx frames rotate and change color between exposures.
  • We tested an AI vision model as a vetter on 47 blind cases. It scored 37 against 43 for a simple measurement, so we shipped no AI.
  • We tested Planet Nine instead of promising it. Passes a year apart cancel the parallax, so we use the pair of passes with the largest jump.
  • We prefer one candidate we can defend over a long list we cannot.

What Afterglow cannot see yet

  • Bright stars saturate the detector and lose their spectrum.
  • Motion under about 3 arcsec between passes is not claimed.
  • Very faint movers, like the brown dwarf WISE 0855, are missed.
  • Spectra are partial: about 25 of 102 channels per star in our field.
  • Planet Nine is about 50 times too faint for one pass.
  • SPHEREx data through Sep 22, 2026, new releases are added by configuration.
